content: Influential educational psychologists and theorists have been recognized for their significant contributions to the field. These individuals include: Albert Bandura (1925–) Alfred Binet (1857–1911) Benjamin Bloom (1913–1999) Ann Brown (1943–1999) Jerome Bruner (1915–) Lee Cronbach (1916–2001) John Dewey (1859–1952) Nathaniel Gage (1917–) Robert Gagné (1916–2002) William James (1842–1910) Maria Montessori (1870–1952) Jean Piaget (1896–1980) Herbert Simon (1916–2001) Burrhus Frederic Skinner (1904–1990) Charles Spearman (1863–1945) Lewis Terman (1877–1956) Edward L. Thorndike (1874–1949) Lev Semenovich Vygotsky (1896–1934) Careers in Educational Psychology Education and Training To become an educational psychologist, one must complete a graduate degree in educational psychology or a closely related field. Universities typically offer graduate programs in educational psychology through psychology departments or, more commonly, faculties of education. Educational psychologists work in diverse settings. Some are employed in universities, where they conduct research on cognitive and social processes related to human development, learning, and education. Others work as consultants, designing and creating educational materials, classroom programs, and online courses. In K-12 school settings, educational psychologists are often referred to as school psychologists in the United States. These professionals are trained at the master’s and doctoral levels. Their responsibilities include conducting assessments and providing services such as academic and behavioral interventions, counseling, teacher consultation, and crisis intervention. In the United Kingdom, becoming a Chartered Educational Psychologist requires: Completing an undergraduate degree in psychology that qualifies for registration with the British Psychological Society. Gaining two to three years of experience working with children, young people, and their families. Completing a three-year professional doctorate in educational psychology. The previous requirement to train and work as a teacher for two years has been discontinued. Employment Outlook The demand for psychologists in the United States is expected to grow faster than the average for most occupations, with an anticipated growth rate of 18–26% through 2014. Approximately one in four psychologists work in educational settings. As of May 2004, the median salary for psychologists in primary and secondary schools in the United States was $58,360. In recent decades, the participation of women as professional researchers in North American educational psychology has increased significantly. The percentage of female authors of peer-reviewed journal articles doubled from 24% in 1976 to 51% in 1995 and has since remained stable. Female membership on editorial boards of educational psychology journals rose from 17% in 1976 to 47% in 2004. Over the same period, the proportion of chief editor positions held by women increased from 22% to 70%. Research Journals A variety of peer-reviewed journals in educational psychology and related fields exist, though the list is not exhaustive. The impact factor of a journal reflects the average number of citations per article published in that journal.
